title: Of Disrespect and Defamation: What Hip Hop Feuds Can Teach Us About the Truth
subtitle: A lawsuit by Drake against Kendrick Lamar got me thinking
body_html:
Welcome to the waning days of the Empire…sorry, the end of 2024. The Frontier Psychiatrists is a health-themed publication that veers routinely into adjacent areas with a profound impact on our well-being. Today, we will cover the crucial domain of defamation law as it applies to beefs in Hip-Hop.

And Baka got a weird case, why is he around?
Certified lover boy, certified pedophiles

—Kendrick Lamar, “Not Like Us”

Nobody likes to be disparaged. Some individuals take particular issue with disrespect to their honor.

American jurisprudence is based on English Common Law—which, at least up through the 1500s generally considered defamation, which includes both spoken content, or slander, and written content, or libel. Way back when, these issues were dealt with by ecclesiastical courts. However, they were limited in the damages they could dole out. It was already understood that insulting somebody's sexuality or sexual preferences was a more grave form of insult than others. Eventually, these cases made their way to the civil courts of the time and proved distressingly popular. Actions were taken to limit what cases plaintiffs could bring, and this led many gentlemen, including here in America, to resolve their disputes with personal violence when their honor was insulted.

We moved, as a society, to bring disputes about false statements into a legal process in response to extra-legal duels. This move to courts arose from violent feuds among the hip-hop stars of yesteryear.

Yes, I am referring to the Founding Fathers! It's more like FWA—Founders With Attitude. You may remember characters like Aaron Burr and Alexander Hamilton? Unlike the cowardly hip-hop stars of today, they didn't do drive-bys. Their diss tracts were published in the newspapers they often ran. When they dissed each other in the popular media of the day, and there was an injury to the honor of one man or another? They would get together, each holding a pistol, turn around, and attempt to shoot each other point-blank in the face.

This is how Hamilton died. There were articles written in a newspaper. Quoting Wikipedia:

When Burr ran for governor of New York in 1804, Hamilton again campaigned against him, arguing that he was unworthy. Taking offense, Burr challenged Hamilton to a duel. In the July 11, 1804, duel in Weehawken, New Jersey, Burr shot Hamilton in the stomach.

Unworthy was a big deal back then. Modern defamation law is an attempt to solve these affronts against someone's honor without needing to shoot each other. One problem for individuals utilizing the legal system to address these concerns? Shooting someone is a rapid way to resolve a dispute. Defamation lawsuits? Less so. Just ask E. Jean Carrol—who’s case is still on appeal. However, in our modern era, defamation is having a real comeback. I’m looking at you, Rudy Giuliani and Alex Jones.

It seems to be that while all other areas of the law can be circumvented with clout, defamation law has held its ground. It’s becoming the way for one citizen to address an injury to their honor by another.

Do you know who likes to insult each other a lot? Rappers. We love free speech in America— but don't allow lies. In fairness, we don't allow for lies that meet the stringent standards of defamation law. In this article, with keen interest, I will review some classic hip-hop-related defamation cases before I get to the big kahuna, the current track by Kendrick Lamar that has led to two separate lawsuits from Mr. Drake.

Fittingly, this article will begin with George Clinton, who we might remember from Parliament Funkadelic. Mr. Clinton was involved in two separate pieces of landmark litigation regarding defamation in a book and, in a second matter, a song he wrote about Armen Boladian:

Brothas Be, Yo Like George, Ain’t That Funkin’ Kinda Hard On You?: A Memoir. Music producer and record label owner Armen Boladian claimed the book defamed him. Boladian’s attorney argued that the book stated that Boladian had “robbed” songs from his client, “fabricated documents,” and “fraudulently backdated and altered agreements.”

The court found in favor of Mr. Clinton twice. The court found, in the matter of his diss track:

… language at issue constituted the kind of "rhetorical hyperbole" that falls outside the ambit of a traditional defamation claim.

and related to claims made in a song called "Speed Dreamin'."

The reference by Clinton to "Armen" in the Lyrics would be understood by such persons as referring to Armen Boladian. The Lyrics, including the statements that refer to the "sorrows and horrors" of Boladian's abuse, that Boladian is a "disgrace to the species", and "got it [killing] comin'" are false and defamatory.

And, the abridged version of the legal opinion is that claiming someone is “a disgrace to the species” is an opinion, not a factual statement made with knowledge that it was false—and thus without requisite malice necessary to overcome a defense to a defamation claim. There are two major defenses to defamation—the first is “what I am saying is true”—that is reporting, and exactly the kind of free speech the consititution is here to protect. The second is that, even if it’s not factually accurate, the statement is a matter of opinion, or the person didn’t know the statement was false, and some more details. In a post-facts world, defamation cases are the last bastion of facts. Importantly, as it will relate to Mr. Lamar and Mr. Drake, the court had an asterisk for us all to consider in the matter of George Clinton dissin’: Their logic was based on the following:

Even speech that is crude — what the Court calls "rhetorical hyperbole,", "vigorous epithet," and "loose, figurative, or hyperbolic language" — merits protection. Id. at 17-21; accord In re Chmura, 464 Mich. 58, 626 N.W.2d 876, 886 (2001)

And follows:

"before a ... public communication is tested for falsity, the communication at issue must involve objectively factual matters"

And found:

There was no specific allegation, such as an act of child abuse, that could be proven; rather, the abuse was the kind of inchoate "loose, figurative" language that the Court referred to in Milkovich. For instance, the statement that "Armen" is a "disgrace to the species," represents the kind of puerile taunt that, for better or worse, is typical of rap music.

Some additional fair on the part of the court that sets a standard—purile taunts = free speech, but “specific allegations such as an action of child abuse” would be outside of the protections due rappers going about their typical business of purile taunting.

Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPP)

It's about time that I briefly mentioned the anti-SLAPP standard, particularly in New York, the country's most active and high-standards defamation jurisdiction.

SLAPP stands for strategic lawsuits against public participation. And an anti-SLAPP motion is the first line of defense against defamation lawsuits designed just to shut up journalists. In New York, which has a lot of opinionated residents and a lot of crooked real estate moguls, it was a frequent strategy of those real estate moguls to sue tenants for saying something defamatory about their shady practices and essentially run them out of money. Instead of being a way to defend your honor, defamation became a tool for the wealthy to silence their critics. So, the anti-SLAPP laws—which don't exist everywhere but definitely exist in the extreme in New York—were created to allow courts to dismiss frivolous lawsuits and recoup legal expenses from the plaintiffs. If, of course, the plaintiffs who brought them didn't have a real chance of winning. This was designed to shut down spurious lawsuits before the case began.

Another quirk of the landscape of defamation law is how frequently homeowners’ insurance handles the defense in those matters. Remember Johnny Depp and Amber Heard? Her homeowners’ insurance paid Amber’s defense! So were Bill Cosby’s, OJ Simpson’s, and Bill Clinton’s. Most homeowners’ policies include indemnification against defamation as part of the policy. These policies come with some interesting clauses, including the ability of the underwriter to recoup all the money they spent on your defense if you're guilty. They don’t underwrite defamation! They're in the business of fulfilling an insurance policy. If someone committed defamation, and it's proved they did? The insurance carrier will then sue the person they were provisionally defending for violating the contract that was their insurance policy—they aren’t indemnified for willful acts.

It costs money to bring a defamation case. It doesn't cost money, out of your own pocket, to defend them if they are frivolous. Usually. Because of the homeowner’s policy indemnification! However, this leads to another asymmetry in that lawyers specializing in prosecuting defamation are experienced. In contrast, insurance-retained non-expert lawyers are on the defense side. Therefore, on average, you'll have more expert lawyers on the prosecution than the defense.

Eminem is Going To Kill You(r Claim That Defamation Occured).

One rapper who has been sued for defamation is Eminem and more than once. In one of the more profound moments of rap defamation, Eminem’s childhood bully sued him for being named in a song as just such a bully:

“Brain Damage” (a song from the 1999 album The Slim Shady LP) [was claimed to be] slanderous. The lyrics read in part: “I was harassed daily by this fat kid named DeAngelo Bailey/He banged my head against the urinal till he broke my nose, soaked my clothes in blood, grabbed me and choked my throat.”

The judge issued her decision in the form of a rap as well, which, I have to say, is dropping it like it’s hot for a judge. Recall, that the “truth” is an absolute defense against a defamation claim:

"Mr. Bailey complains that his rep is trash / So he's seeking compensation in the form of cash / Bailey thinks he's entitled to some monetary gain / Because Eminem used his name in vain / The lyrics are stories no one would take as fact / They're an exaggeration of a childish act / It is therefore this court's ultimate position / That Eminem is entitled to summary disposition."

This decision was upheld on appeal, with the addition of the details highlighting:

In light of plaintiff’s admissions that he “picked on” defendant when defendant was in the fourth grade and that plaintiff was part of a group at school that did “bully type things” such as pushing defendant down, we uphold the trial court’s determination that no genuine issue of material fact was shown relative to this issue.

This is to say that, given the childhood bully's admission that he was a childhood bully, what Eminem said was either reasonably true or an exaggeration that no one would believe to be reporting cold, hard facts.

Eminem’s case and that of Mr. Clinton highlight that defamatory claims will not prevail if they aren’t based on specific factual claims that are demonstrably false and damaging. These are not claims to be brought lightly. However, given the very high standards for plaintiffs to overcome, we should also take rulings against defendants in defamation claims extremely seriously Just ask Alex Jones who just lost InfoWars to the Onion and Rudy Guiliani who just lost his car, watches, a ring and his apartment .

How does this apply to Mr. Drake’s claims against Mr. Lamar?

A Beef, Most Litigious

Kendrick Lamar and Drake do not like each other. This, in hip-hop circles, is known as Beef, and the details of their feud are reviewed in this comprehensive Wikipedia article. The most relevant details follow:

Drake responded with "Family Matters" later on the 3rd, accusing Lamar of being a domestic abuser and alleging that one of Lamar's children was fathered by Dave Free. Less than an hour later, Lamar released "Meet the Grahams,” accusing Drake of sexual predation—including sex trafficking, and fathering a second secret child (in a 2018 diss track by Pusha T, it was revealed that Drake was secretly fathering his son Adonis). Lamar released "Not Like Us" the following day, more explicitly accusing Drake of pedophilia and disrespecting hip-hop.

These are serious claims. Astute readers will notice some issues not present in the above cases, such as Mr. Clinton’s. There are specific claims about specific crimes, including the crime adjacent term pedophilia, and perhaps more importantly, the word certified.

Baka Got A Weird Case

Travis Savoury (born March 6, 1979), known professionally as Baka Not Nice, is the other rapper mentioned by Lamar in the line before he calls both Drake and Baka “Certified lover boy, certified pedophiles.” Mr. Savoury, a long-time member of Drake’s entourage, has a long history of adjudicated criminal behavior:

Travis Savoury pleaded guilty to assaulting a 22-year-old Toronto woman and failing to comply with his recognizance conditions for unrelated Brampton firearms charges, which were withdrawn earlier this year.

Savoury, 37, was sentenced to six months in jail in a Finch Ave. court on April 7, but was allowed to go free since he spent 10 months in custody after his arrest in June 2014.

Charges of procuring for prostitution and human trafficking were dropped.

Including the factually-named Baka Not Nice may cause problems for Mr. Drake’s legal matters. To be clear, Drake alleged RICO violations against I Heart Radio, Spotify, and the Universal Music Group, as well as the underlying defamation claims. The line “certified pedophiles” is especially problematic, and I’ll explain why.

In most defamation cases, you have to prove actual damages. However, some claims are so beyond the pale they are understood to be damaging without needing to prove specific damages.

There are four main ways to classify false statements that the law presumes to be harmful to a person's reputation. If the statement does not fit into one of the four categories, the plaintiff must prove their actual damages.

Here are the four categories of defamation per se:

  1. Saying that someone committed a crime or immoral conduct

  2. Saying that someone had a contagious, infectious, or "loathsome" disease

  3. Saying someone engaged in sexual misconduct or was unchaste

  4. Saying something harmful about someone's business, trade, or profession

The specific claim that Drake and Baka are “certified pedophiles” is likely to be understood to be in the realm of per se defamation—this is the height of immoral conduct and lack of chasity (although this chastity standard only applies to women in New York Law).

The issue for Lamar and the named parties? Not only is this per se defamatory, but it is linked, in the song's lyrics, to Mr. Baka Not Nice and his legal matter. Here, we have actual ground truth—Baka was charged with a crime, convicted, and served time for those crimes. In the law, these are considered true. Lamar raps (with editorial commentary by your author), on “Not Like Us;”

And Party at the party playin' with his nose now

[OM: a reference to the abuse of cocaine and thus futzing with one’s nose]


And Baka got a weird case, why is he around?

[OM: as in case as above, one would reasonably assume]


Certified Lover Boy? Certified pedophiles

[OM: the plural here is crucial, in my opinion]


Wop, wop, wop, wop, wop, Dot, fuck 'em up
Wop, wop, wop, wop, wop, I'ma do my stuff
Why you trollin' like a bitch? Ain't you tired?

[OM: the subsequent lawsuit is prima face evidence of Mr. Drake trollin’ like a b*tch, one could argue]


Tryna strike a chord and it's probably A minor

[OM: this is not defamatory, as he includes the qualifier “probably,” rendering it opinion, and it’s also REALLY FUNNY.]

The legal argument I’d make, in this case, is that Baka’s inclusion is crucial. In Baka’s case, he was convicted of a physical assault on a 22-year-old woman. This is, of course, Not Nice. It is also not a weird case pertaining to the subsequent claim of certified pedophilia—Recall that Baka assaulted an adult. Lamar’s plural links this claim to both men and makes a claim that at least related to Baka, is demonstrably false and misleading. This is the essence of defamation. Lamar knew or should have known this statement was false (it’s in an adjudicated court case). And, per Mr. Clinton’s prior matter, this moves very much past puerile taunts to specific and unsupported claims of sexual assault of children.

Now, there is an out for Lamar—if he can prove that his claims are true, such as in a claim that references activity of the myriad parties thrown by fellow accused pedophile Diddy, then he will have the ultimate defense against the defamation claims.

Now, given both Lamar and Drake are public figures, it is not enough for the damages to be per se—they also have to be made with actual malice.

The dictionary definition of malice is: "the intention or desire to do evil. This intention includes ill-will, hatred or total disregard for the other's well-being." I consider the inability to get fresh fruit in the morning intentional evil on the part of Big Sugar. This statement doesn’t meet the specific legal definition of actual malice:

The defendant either knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth. This means that the defendant entertained serious doubts about the statement's truth.

It’s an even higher standard for public figures! This is where Baka Not Nice’s previous conviction is crucial. Since the track in question is a Diss track—it exists because of ill will, hatred, or total disregard for the other's well-being. That is the point of the diss track. And Lamar knew—or should have known—that Baka’s weird case wasn’t pertaining to a child. Thus, I strongly suspect this rises to the level of actual malice.

Owen Muir, M.D., DFAACAP and The Frontier Psychiatrists as Legal Precedent in Rap Beefs

The extraordinary thing for me, as an author who is a plaintiff in a pending defamation case in New York State revolving around some of the same claims, including those of harming children, is that I am not a casual observer of this case. Depending on who’s matter gets to a decision by the court first; I’m likely going to be referencing Drake v. Lamar (this is not the real name of the case; it’s just amusing to me to write it that way). Alternately, in an bizzare twist of fate, decisions in my case, NYC Psychiatrist Services, P.C. et al. v. Esther Haddad et al., will be cited in the Drake v. Lamar matter as legal precedent. After all, the defendant(s) have accused me of similar, if more gross and baseless, claims:

“Does Bluesky know about the BDSM you do with children” (p. 19)

If you thought the universe couldn't be more odd, I’ll add one more relevant fact. Not only am I in the unenviable position of potentially having my life’s problems and harassment serve as legal precedent in a legal matter related to a rap feud. In addition, this very newsletter? It is being used as evidence in legal filings and has been indexed by Google as an official news source! For that, at least, I am thankful.

Thanks for reading. Now, everyone who has news alerts about defamation, Drake, Kendrick Lamar, or Owen Muir, will get this newsletter pushed to their inbox, too. Happy Thanksgiving, indeed.

The Frontier Psychiatrists is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

The specific claim that Drake and Baka are “certified pedophiles” is likely to be understood to be in the realm of per se defamation—this is the height of immoral conduct and lack of chasity (although this chastity standard only applies to women in New York Law).

The issue for Lamar and the named parties? Not only is this per se defamatory, but it is linked, in the song's lyrics, to Mr. Baka Not Nice and his legal matter . Here, we have actual ground truth—Baka was charged with a crime, convicted, and served time for those crimes. In the law, these are considered true. Lamar raps (with editorial commentary by your author), on “Not Like Us;”

And Party at the party playin' with his nose now

[OM: a reference to the abuse of cocaine and thus futzing with one’s nose]

And Baka got a weird case, why is he around?

[OM: as in case as above, one would reasonably assume]

Certified Lover Boy? Certified pedophiles

[OM: the plural here is crucial, in my opinion]

Wop, wop, wop, wop, wop, Dot, fuck 'em up
Wop, wop, wop, wop, wop, I'ma do my stuff
Why you trollin' like a bitch? Ain't you tired?

[OM: the subsequent lawsuit is prima face evidence of Mr. Drake trollin’ like a b*tch, one could argue]

Tryna strike a chord and it's probably A minor

[OM: this is not defamatory, as he includes the qualifier “probably,” rendering it opinion , and it’s also REALLY FUNNY.]

The legal argument I’d make, in this case, is that Baka’s inclusion is crucial. In Baka’s case, he was convicted of a physical assault on a 22-year-old woman. This is, of course, Not Nice. It is also not a weird case pertaining to the subsequent claim of certified pedophilia—Recall that Baka assaulted an adult . Lamar’s plural links this claim to both men and makes a claim that at least related to Baka, is demonstrably false and misleading. This is the essence of defamation. Lamar knew or should have known this statement was false (it’s in an adjudicated court case ). And, per Mr. Clinton’s prior matter, this moves very much past puerile taunts to specific and unsupported claims of sexual assault of children.

Now, there is an out for Lamar—if he can prove that his claims are true, such as in a claim that references activity of the myriad parties thrown by fellow accused pedophile Diddy, then he will have the ultimate defense against the defamation claims.

Now, given both Lamar and Drake are public figures, it is not enough for the damages to be per se—they also have to be made with actual malice .

The dictionary definition of malice is: "the intention or desire to do evil. This intention includes ill-will, hatred or total disregard for the other's well-being." I consider the inability to get fresh fruit in the morning intentional evil on the part of Big Sugar . This statement doesn’t meet the specific legal definition of actual malice:

The defendant either knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth. This means that the defendant entertained serious doubts about the statement's truth.

It’s an even higher standard for public figures! This is where Baka Not Nice’s previous conviction is crucial. Since the track in question is a Diss track—it exists because of ill will, hatred, or total disregard for the other's well-being. That is the point of the diss track. And Lamar knew—or should have known—that Baka’s weird case wasn’t pertaining to a child. Thus, I strongly suspect this rises to the level of actual malice.
